analysis.one_liner: Caps fees and interest on consumer credit at 36 percent a year and voids loans that exceed it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2014 with 49 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a vote in the House Financial Services Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal crime to lend to a consumer at an effective rate above 36 percent a year, counting every fee—late fees, overdraft fees, credit insurance, add-on products—toward that cap. It would have let borrowers who were overcharged keep the money and void the loan, let state attorneys general sue violators, and required credit card statements to show an all-in "FAIR" rate instead of the APR. It never got a hearing or a vote in the House committee it was assigned to.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who use payday loans, car title loans, overdraft lines, and high-fee credit cards—disproportionately low-income and cash-strapped households paying effective rates of 100 percent to 3,500 percent under the bill's own findings. It also protects the small share of credit card customers hit with heavy penalty fees, and state attorneys general gain a new enforcement tool.

how_it_helps.text: It sets a national maximum 'fee and interest rate' of 36 percent, counting late fees, overdraft fees, cash advance fees, credit insurance, and add-on products—not just the sticker APR—so lenders cannot evade the cap with junk fees.

If a lender violates the cap, the loan becomes unenforceable: the borrower owes back the principal but the creditor must refund interest, fees, and security interests; violations carry criminal penalties of one year in prison and fines of up to triple the accrued debt or $50,000.

It empowers state Attorneys General to sue violators, and it closes federal preemption loopholes that let banks export high rates from states that allow them, while leaving state laws that protect consumers more untouched.
It requires credit card statements to display the all-in cost as a 'FAIR' rate instead of the traditional APR, so borrowers can see what fees really cost.

analysis.who_pays: Payday, car title, installment, and overdraft lenders, plus banks and card issuers that earn large shares of revenue from late fees, over-limit fees, and penalty pricing. Some subprime borrowers who could not qualify for credit under a 36 percent cap would lose access to any formal loan.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday and overdraft lenders, card issuers

drawbacks.text: A hard 36 percent cap on all fees could push borrowers with poor credit out of legal credit entirely, leaving them with no small-dollar loan option at all if lenders cannot price for the risk.

Lenders warned-style objection: because the cap counts every fee (overdraft, late, credit insurance, membership fees), banks would have to stop or radically reprice overdraft lines and other small-balance products that are only viable at high effective rates, shrinking a form of short-term liquidity some households rely on.

Criminal penalties of one year in prison and fines up to triple the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation go beyond typical civil consumer-protection enforcement and could deter lenders from serving marginal borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—ending 100%-to-3,500%-effective interest charges on the poorest borrowers—far outweighed the main costs: some consumers with poor credit would lose access to small-dollar credit entirely or have to turn to informal lenders, and lenders would earn less on high-risk lending. The bill addressed this by permitting modest application and late-fee tolerances and by expressing no bar to affordable small-dollar installment products. Its fatal weakness was political: it never received so much as a committee vote, so its design was never tested in negotiation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote there, and died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Introduced July 17, 2014, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further House action was taken; the committee never marked it up and the House never voted on it.
It ended the Congress with 49 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Republican support.

The bill's own findings put the cost of high-cost lending at roughly $23.7 billion a year in overdraft fees, up to $8.1 billion in payday loans, and rates averaging 400 percent for payday loans and up to 3,500 percent for overdrafts—costs that continued after the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, car title, overdraft, and other high-cost lenders kept charging triple-digit effective rates, saving roughly $30 billion a year in consumer fees from any restriction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost lenders kept charging triple-digit rates

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to establish a national 36 percent usury cap covering all fees, with criminal penalties and state attorney general enforcement.

for.name: 49 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Clyburn, Cummings, Ellison, Clay, and George Miller.

against.name: Payday, car title, and high-cost consumer lending industry
against.what_they_did: High-cost lending trade associations historically opposed federal 36 percent rate caps, and no pro-bill momentum emerged in the committee to overcome that opposition; the bill drew no Republican cosponsors and was never scheduled for a markup.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: The committee took no action on the bill—no hearing, no markup, no vote—leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republicans supported the bill, which never advanced in the Republican-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Payday, car title, and online installment lenders
industries.note: The bill outlaws their core product: loans carrying triple-digit effective rates. It would largely eliminate storefront and online payday lending as it existed, cutting off roughly $8 billion a year in fee revenue collected mostly from low-income borrowers.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and large banks
industries.note: Card issuers that rely on late fees, over-limit fees, and penalty pricing to generate large shares of revenue would face a hard 36 percent ceiling on the sum of those charges. Many mainstream issuers already stayed under the cap for most customers, so the burden fell hardest on subprime and fee-heavy products.

industries.industry: Bank overdraft programs and deposit-advance lenders
industries.note: The bill counts overdraft and insufficient-funds fees toward the 36 percent cap, which would end the practice of effectively charging hundreds of percent annualized on small overdrafts—fees the bill's findings put at roughly $23.7 billion a year.
